what: Morbraii listening prototype — how much of the receive test set has actually been run
source: receive-lab/results.json — 19 rows measured with headless Chromium using a test WAV as the fake microphone, and case 17 measured through the page's own decoder-simulation path
updatedBy: engineer (case 17 re-run after the flush-window fix)

fields.casesRun: cases with a browser result of any kind (decoded or refused)
fields.casesRefused: cases where the decoder declined to name a letter on purpose
fields.casesNotRun: cases with no result at all — not failures, simply never launched
fields.casesInconclusive: cases attempted but which produced no scoreable message
fields.lettersCorrect / lettersScored: positional letter accuracy over the cases that decoded
fields.exactStrings / stringsScored: whole messages that came out exactly right, over the cases that ran
fields.casesCorrect: alias of exactStrings, kept for convenience
fields.maxConfidenceSeen: highest confidence the decoder gave itself on any run so far, in percent
fields.confidenceBarForAsserting: the decoder's own bar: below this it labels a decode tentative, not asserted

notes: Headers are counts only; no number on the listening page is hard-coded, so a future sweep updates this file alone.
This file is fetched by /receive-lab.html at load. It must stay valid JSON and keep these key names.

All 20 cases have now been run. Cases 01, 02, 06, 10, 14, 16 were measured 2026-10-10, case 15 is inconclusive (it produced no scoreable message), the other 12 were measured 2026-10-17 with the same harness, and case 17 was re-run on 2026-10-19 through the page's own decoder-simulation path. All rows, with the method and date each came from, are in receive-lab/results.json.

The five failures are recorded as failures: 09 (SOS at 8 wpm inferred a unit 3.06x too long and printed no letter), 10 and 11 (SOS -> DOS under 12 dB and 6 dB noise), 12 (a false onset 0.7 s early made SOS read ESOS, at the highest confidence in the set, 60%), 14 (reverb, SOS -> ?N).

Case 17 (two elements) used to be a fourth refusal, and the refusal was the page's fault, not the decoder's: the capture window closed after 1000 ms of silence while a 5 wpm word gap is 1680 ms, so the message was cut in half after its first element. With the window at 2500 ms the same recording decodes E T in one message, 2/2 letters, confidence 36% — under the 60% bar, so the page shows it as tentative, and 36% is a fit-error readout, not a probability of being right.

Nothing here was measured on a phone, in a room, with a real buzzer or with a human hand — every case is a synthetic WAV, either injected as Chromium's capture device (19 rows) or pushed straight into the decoder in memory (case 17).
